title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Explain the basic ideas behind ASCII, Unicode, and UTF-8.
Distinguish between characters, Unicode code points, and bytes.
Use Python strings and common string operations to process text.
Use lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets to represent collections of information.
Choose an appropriate data structure based on the operations a problem requires.
Use conditional statements and Boolean logic to control program execution.
Use for and while loops to repeat computations.
Use range() and list comprehensions to construct and process collections.
Break a computational problem into a sequence of precise steps.
Explain what an algorithm is and why algorithmic efficiency matters.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
ASCII
The earliest widely used character encoding schemes included ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
ASCII assigns numbers to a relatively small collection of characters:

ord("A")

65



ord("a")

97



ord("0")

48


The inverse operation is chr():

chr(65)

'A'



chr(97)

'a'


ASCII is useful, but it has an important limitation: it contains only a small number of characters.
It can represent English letters, digits, punctuation, and various control characters, but it cannot represent the world’s writing systems.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Unicode
Unicode is a much larger system designed to assign code points to characters from languages and writing systems around the world.
For example:

ord("A")

65



ord("é")

233



ord("中")

20013


Notice that a Unicode code point is just an integer.
We can convert it back to a character:

chr(233)

'é'



chr(20013)

'中'








Important



A character’s Unicode code point is not necessarily the same thing as the sequence of bytes used to store that character.
This distinction becomes important when we work with files and data from different sources.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
UTF-8
Unicode tells us which numerical code point corresponds to a character. We still need a way to represent that information as bytes.
UTF-8 is a widely used encoding for doing this.
Python allows us to encode a string into bytes:

text = "Hello"
encoded = text.encode("utf-8")

encoded

b'Hello'


We can inspect the individual bytes:

list(encoded)

[72, 101, 108, 108, 111]


Now consider a string containing a non-ASCII character:

text = "café"
encoded = text.encode("utf-8")

encoded

b'caf\xc3\xa9'



list(encoded)

[99, 97, 102, 195, 169]


The character é is one character, but its UTF-8 representation requires multiple bytes.
We can convert the bytes back into a string using .decode():

encoded.decode("utf-8")

'café'


The general process is:
character
    ↓
Unicode code point
    ↓
UTF-8 encoding
    ↓
bytes
and, in the other direction:
bytes
    ↓
UTF-8 decoding
    ↓
Unicode code point
    ↓
character

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Slicing
We can obtain a portion of a string using a slice:

name[0:3]

'Pyt'


The general form is:
sequence[start:stop]
The start position is included, while the stop position is excluded.
For example:

name[1:4]

'yth'


We can also omit either endpoint:

name[:3]

'Pyt'



name[3:]

'hon'


And we can use a step:

name[::2]

'Pto'



name[::-1]

'nohtyP'

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Strings Are Immutable
An important property of Python strings is that they are immutable.
For example, this does not work:
name[0] = "p"
Instead, operations that appear to modify a string actually create a new string.

name = "Python"

lower_name = name.lower()

name, lower_name

('Python', 'python')


The original string has not changed:

name

'Python'

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
String Methods
Python provides many useful string methods.

text = "  Hello, World!  "


text.strip()

'Hello, World!'



text.lower()

'  hello, world!  '



text.upper()

'  HELLO, WORLD!  '



text.replace("World", "Python")

'  Hello, Python!  '



text.split(",")

['  Hello', ' World!  ']


We can also test properties of strings:

"12345".isdigit()

True



"Hello".isalpha()

True



"hello".startswith("he")

True



"hello".endswith("lo")

True

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Lists
A list is an ordered, mutable collection.

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

We can index a list:

numbers[0]

10


and slice it:

numbers[1:4]

[20, 30, 40]


We can change an element:

numbers[0] = 99

numbers

[99, 20, 30, 40, 50]


We can append an element:

numbers.append(60)

numbers

[99, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]


We can remove an element:

numbers.remove(30)

numbers

[99, 20, 40, 50, 60]


Lists can contain different types of objects:

example = [1, "hello", 3.14, True]

But in practice, a list will often contain objects of the same general type.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Tuples
A tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence.

point = (3, 4)

We can access its elements:

point[0]

3


But we cannot change them:
point[0] = 5
The distinction between lists and tuples is therefore partly about whether the collection should be mutable.






Note



Do not memorize a rule such as “always use a list” or “always use a tuple.”
Instead, ask what your data represent and what operations your program needs to perform.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Dictionaries
A dictionary stores key-value pairs.

student = {
    "name": "Alice",
    "age": 24,
    "program": "Mathematics"
}

We can retrieve a value using its key:

student["name"]

'Alice'



student["age"]

24


We can add or change entries:

student["year"] = 1

student

{'name': 'Alice', 'age': 24, 'program': 'Mathematics', 'year': 1}


Dictionaries are particularly useful when we want to associate one piece of information with another.
For example:
student ID → student name
country → population
word → frequency
stock ticker → price
This is why a dictionary is a natural choice for our character-frequency problem.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Character Frequency with a Dictionary
Consider:

text = "banana"

We want to construct:
b → 1
a → 3
n → 2
One way to describe the algorithm is:

Start with an empty dictionary.
Examine each character.
If the character has not appeared before, initialize its count to zero.
Increase its count by one.
Continue until all characters have been processed.

Let’s implement this directly.

text = "banana"

counts = {}

for character in text:
    if character not in counts:
        counts[character] = 0

    counts[character] += 1

counts

{'b': 1, 'a': 3, 'n': 2}


Notice what we have done.
We have taken an informal problem—

“Count how frequently each character occurs.”

—and translated it into a precise sequence of computational steps.
That is algorithmic thinking.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow

text:
Choosing a Data Structure
Consider the following problems.

Problem 1
We need to store the names of students in the order in which they submitted an assignment.
Possible choice: list.


Problem 2
We need to associate each student ID with the student’s name.
Possible choice: dictionary.


Problem 3
We need to determine which students submitted an assignment, without caring about submission order.
Possible choice: set.


Problem 4
We need to store the coordinates of a point (x, y) and do not want those coordinates to change.
Possible choice: tuple.






Important



The important programming skill is not memorizing the four data structures.
It is learning to ask:

What operations does my problem require, and which data structure naturally supports those operations?

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Conditional Statements
The basic structure is:
if condition:
    statement
For example:

x = 10

if x > 0:
    print("positive")

positive


We can add an alternative:

x = -3

if x > 0:
    print("positive")
else:
    print("not positive")

not positive


And multiple possibilities:

x = 0

if x > 0:
    print("positive")
elif x < 0:
    print("negative")
else:
    print("zero")

zero

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Boolean Logic
Conditions evaluate to True or False.

x = 10

x > 0

True



x == 10

True



x != 5

True


We can combine conditions using and, or, and not.

x > 0 and x < 20

True



x < 0 or x > 100

False



not (x == 10)

False

text:
for Loops
A for loop repeats an operation over the elements of a collection.

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

for number in numbers:
    print(number)

10
20
30
40


The loop variable takes on each value in sequence.
We can perform computations inside the loop:

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

for number in numbers:
    print(number ** 2)

100
400
900
1600


We can combine loops with conditionals:

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

for number in numbers:
    if number % 2 == 0:
        print(number)

2
4
6

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
while Loops
A while loop repeats as long as a condition remains true.

x = 1

while x <= 5:
    print(x)
    x += 1

1
2
3
4
5


A while loop is useful when we do not know in advance exactly how many iterations will be required.
For example:

x = 1

while x < 100:
    x *= 2

x

128


Be careful: if the condition never becomes false, the loop will never terminate.






Warning



Infinite loops are a common programming error.
Whenever you write a while loop, ask:

What changes during each iteration that will eventually make the condition false?

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
From Problem to Algorithm
Consider the problem:

Given a list of numbers, determine the largest value.

A natural algorithm is:

Start with the first value as the current maximum.
Examine the next value.
If it is larger than the current maximum, make it the new maximum.
Continue until every value has been examined.
Return the maximum.

We can implement this directly:

numbers = [7, 3, 12, 5, 9]

current_max = numbers[0]

for number in numbers[1:]:
    if number > current_max:
        current_max = number

current_max

12


Python of course already provides:

max(numbers)

12


But implementing the algorithm ourselves is useful because it forces us to understand the underlying procedure.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Breaking Problems into Smaller Steps
A useful strategy for complicated computational problems is to break them into smaller problems.
For example, suppose we want to determine the average of all positive values in a list.
Rather than thinking:

“Write a program that calculates the average of positive values.”

Break it down:

Identify the positive values.
Add them together.
Count them.
Divide the sum by the count.

Each step is easier to implement and test independently.

values = [-2, 4, 7, -1, 5, 0, 3]

# Your code here

This idea—decomposition—will become increasingly important as our programs become more complicated.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Exercise: Compare Two Algorithms
Suppose we want to determine whether a particular value occurs in a list.
A straightforward approach is to examine the elements one at a time:

numbers = list(range(100))

target = 73

found = False

for number in numbers:
    if number == target:
        found = True
        break

found

True


Python also provides:

target in numbers

True


Now consider what happens if we need to perform this membership test thousands or millions of times.
Would a list always be the best data structure?
Think back to sets.

numbers_set = set(numbers)

target in numbers_set

True


This is an example of a broader principle:

The choice of algorithm and data structure can determine whether a computational problem is easy or difficult at scale.

We will return to this idea throughout the course.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Text and Encoding

Computers ultimately store information as bits and bytes.
Unicode assigns code points to characters.
UTF-8 provides a way to encode Unicode characters as bytes.
A character, a code point, and its byte representation are related but distinct concepts.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Data Structures
Python provides several fundamental ways to organize collections of information:








Data structure
Key property
Typical use




list
Ordered, mutable
Sequence of observations


tuple
Ordered, immutable
Fixed collection such as coordinates


dict
Key-value mapping
Associations and counts


set
Unique elements
Membership and uniqueness



The appropriate data structure depends on the operations your problem requires.

title: Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
Lecture 2: Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Algorithms
An algorithm is a precise procedure for solving a problem.
A useful workflow is:
Problem
→ specification
→ algorithm
→ implementation
→ testing
→ result
We also saw that different algorithms can require very different amounts of computational work.

text:
Step 1: Install Python and Run from Terminal

1.1 Download and Install Python
First, we need to install Python on your system. We’ll install the latest stable version.

WindowsMacLinux



Visit python.org
Download the latest Python 3.x installer for Windows
IMPORTANT: Run the installer and check the box that says “Add Python to PATH” at the bottom of the first screen
Click “Install Now”
Wait for installation to complete







WarningCritical Step!



If you forget to check “Add Python to PATH”, you’ll need to either: - Uninstall and reinstall Python (checking the box this time), OR - Manually add Python to your PATH environment variable






Visit python.org
Download the latest Python 3.x installer for macOS
Open the downloaded .pkg file
Follow the installation wizard (accept defaults)
Python will be automatically added to your PATH







NotemacOS Note



macOS comes with Python 2.7 pre-installed (older versions) or Python 3 (newer versions). We’re installing the latest version to ensure you have all modern features.





Most Linux distributions come with Python 3 pre-installed. To install the latest version:
Ubuntu/Debian:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3 python3-pip python3-venv
Fedora:
sudo dnf install python3 python3-pip
Arch Linux:
sudo pacman -S python python-pip





1.2 Test Your Installation
Let’s verify that Python is installed correctly and accessible from your terminal.

WindowsMacLinux



Open PowerShell (search for “PowerShell” in the Start menu)
Type the following command and press Enter:

python --version
You should see something like Python 3.12.0 (version number may vary).



Open Terminal (Applications → Utilities → Terminal, or search “Terminal”)
Type the following command and press Enter:

python3 --version
You should see something like Python 3.12.0 (version number may vary).



Open your terminal application
Type the following command and press Enter:

python3 --version
You should see something like Python 3.12.0 (version number may vary).






1.3 Running Python Interactively
One of the most powerful ways to learn Python is through the interactive interpreter (also called the REPL - Read-Eval-Print Loop). This lets you type Python commands one at a time and see immediate results.

WindowsMac/Linux


In PowerShell, type:
python


In Terminal, type:
python3



You should see something like this:
Python 3.12.0 (main, Oct 10 2023, 12:00:00)
[GCC 9.4.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>>
The >>> is the Python prompt, waiting for your input.


1.4 Exploring Basic Python Concepts
Now let’s explore some fundamental Python concepts. Type each command after the >>> prompt.

Variables and Dynamic Typing
Python uses dynamic typing, meaning variables can hold different types of data at different times:

# Integer
x = 10
type(x)  # Returns: <class 'int'>


# String
x = 'phil'
type(x)  # Returns: <class 'str'>


# Float
x = 10.0
type(x)  # Returns: <class 'float'>


# Boolean (note: must be capitalized!)
x = True
type(x)  # Returns: <class 'bool'>







ImportantPython is Case-Sensitive!



Try typing x = TrUe (wrong capitalization):

x = TrUe  # This will raise a NameError!

This produces an error because Python expects True with capital T and lowercase r, u, e.




Working with Multiple Variables

x = 10
y = 20



Checking Your Workspace
The dir() function shows all variables and functions currently in your workspace:

dir()

You’ll see a list that includes x and y along with some built-in names.


Importing Modules
Python’s power comes from its extensive library of modules. Let’s use the math module:

import math
math.sin(0)  # Returns: 0.0

The sine of 0 radians is 0 (as expected from trigonometry).


Exiting Python
To exit the interactive interpreter:

quit()

Or press Ctrl+D (Mac/Linux) or Ctrl+Z then Enter (Windows).






TipWhat We Just Learned




Python uses dynamic typing (variables can change types)
type() tells us what kind of data we have
dir() shows what’s in our workspace
Python has many built-in modules like math
Python is case-sensitive!

Step 2: Create Folder Structure and Run a Python Script
While the interactive interpreter is great for experimentation, real programming happens in script files that we can save, edit, and run repeatedly.

2.1 Create Your Course Folder Structure

mkdir math5200

# Navigate into it
cd math5200

# Create a subfolder for source code
mkdir src

# Verify the structure
ls









NoteWhy ‘src’?



The src folder is a common convention meaning “source code”. Keeping your code organized from the start is a professional habit that will serve you well.




2.2 Create Your First Python Script
Now let’s create a Python script file.

WindowsMacLinux


You can use any text editor. Let’s use Notepad for simplicity:
# Make sure you're in the math5200 directory
cd $HOME\Documents\math5200\src

# Open Notepad (or use your preferred text editor)
notepad first_script.py


You can use TextEdit or any text editor:
# Make sure you're in the math5200 directory
cd ~/Documents/math5200/src

# Open TextEdit (or use nano, vim, etc.)
open -a TextEdit first_script.py
Or use a command-line editor:
nano first_script.py


Use your preferred text editor:
# Make sure you're in the math5200 directory
cd ~/Documents/math5200/src

# Use nano (simple) or vim, gedit, etc.
nano first_script.py





2.3 Write Your First Script
In the text editor, type the following Python code:

# first_script.py
# My first Python script!

print("Hello, Python world!")
print("=" * 40)  # Print a line of 40 equals signs

# Define some variables
name = "Student"
course = "Math 5200"
year = 2026

# Print formatted information
print(f"Welcome, {name}!")
print(f"Course: {course}")
print(f"Year: {year}")
print("=" * 40)

# Do some calculations
x = 10
y = 20
sum_result = x + y
product = x * y

print(f"{x} + {y} = {sum_result}")
print(f"{x} × {y} = {product}")

# Import a module and use it
import math
angle_rad = math.pi / 4  # 45 degrees in radians
sin_value = math.sin(angle_rad)

print("=" * 40)
print(f"sin(π/4) = {sin_value:.4f}")
print("Script complete!")

Save the file and close the editor.






TipUnderstanding the Code




print() displays text to the console
"=" * 40 repeats the equals sign 40 times (string multiplication)
f"..." creates an f-string (formatted string) where {variable} is replaced with the variable’s value
{sin_value:.4f} formats the number to 4 decimal places





2.4 Run Your Script
Now let’s run the script from the terminal.

WindowsMac/Linux


In PowerShell:
# Make sure you're in the src directory
cd $HOME\Documents\math5200\src

# Run the script
python first_script.py


In Terminal:
# Make sure you're in the src directory
cd ~/Documents/math5200/src

# Run the script
python3 first_script.py



You should see output like:
Hello, Python world!
========================================
Welcome, Student!
Course: Math 5200
Year: 2026
========================================
10 + 20 = 30
10 × 20 = 200
========================================
sin(π/4) = 0.7071
Script complete!







TipWhat We Just Learned




Python scripts are just text files with a .py extension
We run scripts by typing python scriptname.py (or python3 on Mac/Linux)
Scripts execute from top to bottom
Everything we can do interactively, we can do in a script

text:
Step 4: Create Virtual Environment and Use with Spyder
Now we’ll create our first virtual environment. Think of a virtual environment as a separate Python installation specific to a project, with its own set of packages.

4.1 Understanding Virtual Environments






NoteWhy Virtual Environments?



Imagine you have: - Project A that needs numpy version 1.24 - Project B that needs numpy version 1.26 (with breaking changes)
Without virtual environments, you can only have one version installed globally. With virtual environments, each project gets its own Python installation with its own packages!




4.2 Create Your First Virtual Environment
Let’s create a virtual environment called env1.

WindowsMac/Linux


# Navigate to your course folder
cd $HOME\Documents\math5200

# Create a virtual environment named 'env1'
python -m venv env1

# Activate the virtual environment
.\env1\Scripts\Activate.ps1






WarningPowerShell Execution Policy



If you get an error about execution policies, run:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
Then try activating again.




# Navigate to your course folder
cd ~/Documents/math5200

# Create a virtual environment named 'env1'
python3 -m venv env1

# Activate the virtual environment
source env1/bin/activate



When activated, you’ll see (env1) at the beginning of your command prompt:
(env1) PS C:\Users\YourName\Documents\math5200>
This indicates you’re working inside the virtual environment.



4.3 Install Required Packages
Now we’ll install packages specifically for this virtual environment.

# Upgrade pip (good practice)
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

# Install spyder-kernels (required to connect Spyder to this environment)
pip install spyder-kernels







NoteWhat is spyder-kernels?



spyder-kernels is a bridge that allows Spyder (running globally) to execute code in your virtual environment. Without it, Spyder can’t “see” your environment’s Python installation.




4.4 Find Your Virtual Environment’s Python Path
We need to tell Spyder where this environment’s Python is located. Let’s find the path:

WindowsMac/Linux


# While env1 is activated
(Get-Command python).Path
Or:
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
This will output something like:
C:\Users\YourName\Documents\math5200\env1\Scripts\python.exe
Copy this path - you’ll need it in the next step!


# While env1 is activated
which python3
Or:
python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
This will output something like:
/Users/YourName/Documents/math5200/env1/bin/python3
Copy this path - you’ll need it in the next step!









TipFinding All Python Installations



To see all Python installations on your system:
Windows (PowerShell):
py -0p  # If Python Launcher is installed
Mac/Linux:
# Find Python in common locations
which -a python python3
ls /usr/bin/python*
ls /usr/local/bin/python*




4.5 Connect Spyder to Your Virtual Environment
Now let’s configure Spyder to use our env1 virtual environment.






ImportantStep-by-Step Instructions



Follow these steps carefully. We’ll make the configuration persistent so it applies every time you start a new console.



Open Spyder (if not already open)
Go to Preferences:

Windows/Linux: Tools → Preferences
Mac: Python → Preferences (or Spyder → Preferences)








ImportantMac Users: Finding Preferences



On Mac, Preferences is not under Tools! Instead:

Menu bar (top of screen): Spyder → Preferences… OR Python → Preferences…
Keyboard shortcut: ⌘, (Command + comma)
Can’t find it? Help → Spyder tutorial → search “Preferences” → Enter

The location is in the menu bar at the top of your screen, not in Spyder’s window!



Navigate to Python Interpreter:

In the left sidebar, click Python interpreter

Select “Use the following Python interpreter”:

Click the radio button for “Use the following Python interpreter”
Click the text box or the folder icon to browse

Paste Your Python Path:

Paste the path you copied earlier (e.g., C:\Users\YourName\Documents\math5200\env1\Scripts\python.exe on Windows)
Click OK or Apply

Restart Spyder:

Close and reopen Spyder for changes to take effect
Alternatively, go to Consoles → Restart kernel in an open console









TipVerifying the Connection



After restarting, you can verify which Python Spyder is using by typing in the IPython console:
import sys
print(sys.executable)
You should see the path to your env1 Python!




4.5.1 Troubleshooting: Spyder-Kernels Version Compatibility






WarningCommon Issue: Version Mismatch



When you first try to use Spyder with your virtual environment, you might see an error message like:
The Python environment or installation whose interpreter is located at

    C:\Users\YourName\Documents\math5200\env1\Scripts\python.exe

doesn't have the spyder-kernels module or the right version of it installed 
(>= 2.4.0 and < 2.5.0). Without this module is not possible for Spyder to 
create a console for you.

You can install it by activating your environment (if necessary) and 
then running in a system terminal:

    conda install spyder-kernels=2.4
or
    pip install spyder-kernels==2.4.*
Don’t panic! This is completely normal and easy to fix.



Why Does This Happen?
The issue occurs because Spyder (the IDE you installed globally) and spyder-kernels (the bridge you installed in your virtual environment) need to have compatible versions.
Think of it like this: - Spyder is like a remote control (installed globally on your system) - spyder-kernels is like a receiver (installed in each virtual environment) - The remote and receiver need to “speak the same language” (compatible versions)
When you install Spyder globally, it expects a specific range of spyder-kernels versions. If you simply run pip install spyder-kernels in your virtual environment, you might get the latest version, which could be too new or too old for your version of Spyder.


How to Fix It
The error message helpfully tells you exactly what to do! Follow these steps:
Step 1: Note the required version from the error message
Look for the version requirement in the error. It will say something like: - >= 2.4.0 and < 2.5.0 (meaning version 2.4.x) - Or it might directly suggest: spyder-kernels==2.4.*
Step 2: Activate your virtual environment (if not already active)

WindowsMac/Linux


cd $HOME\Documents\math5200
.\env1\Scripts\Activate.ps1


cd ~/Documents/math5200
source env1/bin/activate



Step 3: Install the compatible version
Use the exact command suggested in the error message. For example:

# Install the specific version range that Spyder needs
pip install spyder-kernels==2.4.*

Or if a more specific version is suggested:

pip install spyder-kernels==2.4.3

The ==2.4.* syntax means “install any version that is 2.4.something” (like 2.4.0, 2.4.1, 2.4.3, etc.)
Step 4: Restart Spyder or the kernel

Close and reopen Spyder, OR
In Spyder: Consoles → Restart kernel (or press Ctrl+.)

The error should now be gone!


Checking Versions
You can check which versions you have installed:
Check Spyder version:
In Spyder’s console (or any Python console):

import spyder
print(spyder.__version__)

Or from the terminal:
# Windows
spyder --version

# Mac/Linux
spyder --version
Check spyder-kernels version (in your virtual environment):

# Make sure your virtual environment is activated first!
pip show spyder-kernels

This shows you detailed information including the version number.


Preventing This Issue
To avoid version mismatches in the future:
Option 1: Install the compatible version immediately (Recommended)
When setting up a new virtual environment, install the compatible spyder-kernels version right away:

# Activate your environment first
# Then check what version your global Spyder needs
# For example, if you have Spyder 5.4.x:
pip install spyder-kernels==2.4.*

Option 2: Keep Spyder updated
Periodically update your global Spyder installation:
pip install --upgrade spyder
Then update spyder-kernels in your virtual environments to match.

You might wonder: “Why not just install Spyder itself in each virtual environment?”
You can do this! Some people prefer this approach because it guarantees compatibility. However:
Pros of global Spyder: - Only one installation to maintain - Less disk space used - Same familiar Spyder interface across all projects
Pros of per-environment Spyder: - Perfect version matching every time - Complete project isolation - Can use different Spyder versions for different projects

If you’ve installed the correct spyder-kernels version and still see errors:

# In your virtual environment
import sys
print(sys.executable)  # Should point to your virtual environment

4.6 Tour of Spyder
Now that Spyder is connected to your virtual environment, let’s explore its interface.

Spyder has several key panels:

1. Editor (Left side)

This is where you write and edit your Python scripts
Multiple files can be open in tabs
Features syntax highlighting, code completion, and real-time error checking



2. IPython Console (Bottom right)

Interactive Python console (like the terminal, but better!)
Results appear immediately after you type commands
Access to command history
Rich output (plots, tables, etc.)



3. Variable Explorer (Top right)

Shows all variables currently in memory
Double-click to view/edit variable contents
See data types, sizes, and values at a glance
This is incredibly useful for debugging and understanding program state!



4. Help/Plots Pane (Top right, tabs)

Help: Documentation for functions/objects (press Ctrl+I when cursor is on a function)
Plots: Displays matplotlib plots inline
Files: Browse your file system




4.7 Working in Spyder
Let’s write and run some code in Spyder.

Using the Editor

In the Editor panel, create a new file (File → New File or Ctrl+N)
Type the following code:


# spyder_demo.py
# Demonstrating Spyder features

import math

# Create some variables
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
squared = [x**2 for x in numbers]

# Calculate statistics
total = sum(numbers)
mean = total / len(numbers)
std_dev = math.sqrt(sum((x - mean)**2 for x in numbers) / len(numbers))

# Print results
print(f"Numbers: {numbers}")
print(f"Squared: {squared}")
print(f"Mean: {mean}")
print(f"Standard Deviation: {std_dev:.3f}")

# Create a dictionary

    'numbers': numbers,
    'squared': squared,
    'mean': mean,
    'std_dev': std_dev
}

Save the file (File → Save or Ctrl+S) in your math5200/src folder as spyder_demo.py
Run the file:

Click the green “Run” triangle button in the toolbar, OR
Press F5, OR
Go to Run → Run





Observe the Results

Variable Explorer: See all your variables (numbers, squared, total, mean, std_dev, data)

Click on numbers to see the list
Click on data to see the dictionary contents








TipVariable Explorer Power



The Variable Explorer is one of Spyder’s best features! You can: - See all variables and their types/sizes - Double-click to view contents in detail - Edit simple variables directly - Export data to files




Using the Console Interactively
In the IPython Console, you can interact with the variables from your script:

# These variables exist because we ran the script

# Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# Output: 9

# Output: 3.0

Let’s install numpy, a fundamental package for scientific computing.

From TerminalFrom Spyder Console

You can also install packages directly from Spyder’s IPython console:

The ! tells IPython to run a system command.

After installing a new package, you need to restart the Python kernel to use it.

import numpy as np

# Create a numpy array
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
print(arr)
print(f"Array type: {type(arr)}")

# Perform vectorized operations

Python loads modules into memory when you first import them. To see newly installed packages, you need to restart the Python process (kernel) so it can find and load the new packages.

When you’re done working, you can deactivate the virtual environment.

Step 5: Create a Second Virtual Environment
Now let’s create a second virtual environment to demonstrate package isolation - the key benefit of virtual environments.

5.1 Create and Activate env2

WindowsMac/Linux


# Navigate to your course folder (if not there)
cd $HOME\Documents\math5200

# Create a new virtual environment
python -m venv env2

# Activate it
.\env2\Scripts\Activate.ps1


# Navigate to your course folder (if not there)
cd ~/Documents/math5200

# Create a new virtual environment
python3 -m venv env2

# Activate it
source env2/bin/activate



You should now see (env2) in your prompt.


5.2 Install Basic Requirements

# Upgrade pip
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

# Install spyder-kernels (required to use with Spyder)
pip install spyder-kernels



5.3 Create a requirements.txt File
A requirements.txt file lists all the packages your project needs. This makes your work reproducible - anyone can recreate your exact environment.
Create a file called requirements.txt in your math5200 folder:

WindowsMacLinux


cd $HOME\Documents\math5200
notepad requirements.txt


cd ~/Documents/math5200
open -a TextEdit requirements.txt
# or
nano requirements.txt


cd ~/Documents/math5200
nano requirements.txt



In the file, add these packages (note: we’re not including numpy):
requests==2.31.0
tabulate==0.9.0






NoteWhat are these packages?




requests: A library for making HTTP requests (useful for fetching data from APIs)
tabulate: A library for creating nicely formatted tables

Both are useful for scientific work but don’t depend on numpy, which will let us demonstrate environment isolation.


Save and close the file.


5.4 Install from requirements.txt

# Install all packages listed in requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt

This installs requests and tabulate but not numpy.


5.5 Connect Spyder to env2
Now let’s switch Spyder to use env2.

5.5.1 Get env2’s Python Path

WindowsMac/Linux


# Make sure env2 is activated
(Get-Command python).Path
Output example: C:\Users\YourName\Documents\math5200\env2\Scripts\python.exe


# Make sure env2 is activated
which python3
Output example: /Users/YourName/Documents/math5200/env2/bin/python3



Copy this path!


5.5.2 Update Spyder’s Interpreter

Open Spyder (if not open)
Go to Tools → Preferences (or Python/Spyder → Preferences on Mac)
Click Python interpreter in the left sidebar
Paste the env2 path into the text box
Click OK or Apply
Restart Spyder or restart the kernel (Consoles → Restart kernel)





5.6 Demonstrate Package Isolation
Now for the important demonstration: env2 has different packages than env1.

Try to import numpy (will fail!)
In Spyder’s console:

import numpy as np

You should get an error:
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'






ImportantThis is Expected!



This error is good! It shows that env2 is completely isolated from env1. Even though we installed numpy in env1, it’s not available in env2. This isolation prevents package conflicts and ensures reproducibility.




Use the packages from env2
Now try using the packages we did install:

import requests
from tabulate import tabulate

# Test requests (fetch some data)
response = requests.get('https://api.github.com')
print(f"GitHub API Status: {response.status_code}")

# Test tabulate (create a nice table)
data = [
    ['env1', 'numpy', 'Yes'],
    ['env1', 'requests', 'No'],
    ['env2', 'numpy', 'No'],
    ['env2', 'requests', 'Yes'],
]
headers = ['Environment', 'Package', 'Installed?']

print("\nPackage Availability:")
print(tabulate(data, headers=headers, tablefmt='grid'))

Expected output:
GitHub API Status: 200

Package Availability:
+---------------+-----------+-------------+
| Environment   | Package   | Installed?  |
+===============+===========+=============+
| env1          | numpy     | Yes         |
+---------------+-----------+-------------+
| env1          | requests  | No          |
+---------------+-----------+-------------+
| env2          | numpy     | No          |
+---------------+-----------+-------------+
| env2          | requests  | Yes         |
+---------------+-----------+-------------+




5.7 Switch Back to env1
To verify, let’s switch back to env1 and show that numpy works there.

Get env1’s Python path again:


WindowsMac/Linux


# Deactivate env2 first
deactivate

# Activate env1
cd $HOME\Documents\math5200
.\env1\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Get path
(Get-Command python).Path


# Deactivate env2 first
deactivate

# Activate env1
cd ~/Documents/math5200
source env1/bin/activate

# Get path
which python3




Update Spyder’s interpreter to env1’s path (same process as before)
Restart Spyder’s kernel
Test:


import numpy as np
print("numpy works in env1!")
print(np.array([1, 2, 3]))

# Try requests (will fail in env1)
import requests  # ModuleNotFoundError!







TipKey Takeaway



Each virtual environment is completely independent. This allows you to: - Use different versions of packages for different projects - Avoid conflicts between incompatible packages - Share exact requirements with collaborators - Reproduce your analysis environment months or years later

Basic Troubleshooting
Here are solutions to common issues you might encounter:

Issue 1: “python: command not found” or “‘python’ is not recognized”
Solution: Python wasn’t added to your PATH during installation.

Windows: Uninstall and reinstall Python, making sure to check “Add Python to PATH”
Mac/Linux: Use python3 instead of python, or create an alias



Issue 2: Can’t activate virtual environment on Windows (Execution Policy error)
Solution:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser


Issue 3: Spyder won’t start or crashes
Solutions: - Make sure you installed spyder-kernels in your virtual environment - Try resetting Spyder’s settings: Help → Reset Spyder to factory defaults - Check Python version compatibility with your Spyder version


Issue 4: Spyder doesn’t see newly installed packages
Solution: Restart the kernel (Consoles → Restart kernel or Ctrl+.)


Issue 5: “ModuleNotFoundError” even though package is installed
Solutions: - Verify you’re using the correct virtual environment in Spyder (check with import sys; print(sys.executable)) - Make sure the package is installed in the active environment: pip list - Restart the kernel after installing packages


Issue 6: Can’t find the Python executable path
Solution: Use Python itself to tell you:

WindowsMac/Linux


python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"


python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"





Issue 7: Multiple Python versions installed - confusion about which is which
Solution:
Windows:
py -0p  # Lists all Python installations
Mac/Linux:
which -a python python3
ls -l /usr/bin/python*
ls -l /usr/local/bin/python*


Issue 8: Virtual environment activated but wrong Python still running
Solution: - Deactivate and reactivate the environment - Check with which python (Mac/Linux) or (Get-Command python).Path (Windows) - Make sure you’re using the activation script from the correct environment folder

Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
Programming is often introduced as the process of learning a programming language. That is only part of the story.
A programming language provides a way to express computations, but effective computational work requires us to think about several additional questions:

How should a problem be represented?
What algorithm should we use?
How should the algorithm be implemented?
How can we determine whether the implementation is correct?
How does the computer represent the quantities involved?
What numerical errors can arise?
How can the computation be reproduced and independently checked?

A useful computational workflow is:
Problem
   ↓
Representation
   ↓
Algorithm
   ↓
Implementation
   ↓
Testing
   ↓
Numerical validation
   ↓
Results
   ↓
Communication / Reproducibility
This course will return to this workflow repeatedly.
A central theme of this first lecture is:

A computer does not manipulate mathematical objects directly. It executes algorithms using finite representations of information.

This distinction is particularly important in numerical work.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
2.1 Algorithms
An algorithm is a finite, well-defined procedure for solving a problem.
For the sum-of-squares problem, one algorithm is:
total ← 0
for i from 1 through n:
    total ← total + i²
return total
Another algorithm uses the closed-form expression:
return n(n+1)(2n+1)/6
The two algorithms solve the same mathematical problem, but they have different computational properties.
The first requires work proportional to \(n\). The second requires a fixed number of high-level arithmetic operations.
This is our first example of an important distinction:

Mathematically equivalent methods need not be computationally equivalent.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
4.1 Mathematical variables
In mathematics, a variable is typically a symbol representing an element of some mathematical domain.
For example,
\[
x \in \mathbb{R}
\]
says that \(x\) is a real number.
An equation such as
\[
x = 10
\]
can be interpreted as a mathematical assertion that \(x\) has value 10.
Programming languages use the word variable, but the concept is somewhat different.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
4.2 Assignment
In Python:
x = 10
is an assignment statement.
A useful conceptual interpretation is:

Evaluate the expression on the right and bind the name on the left to the resulting object.

After:
x = 10
the name x refers to an integer object representing 10.
The statement
x = x + 1
therefore makes sense as a program instruction even though
\[
x = x + 1
\]
would normally be impossible as an equation over ordinary numbers.
Python interprets:
x = x + 1
as:

retrieve the current value associated with x;
add 1;
bind x to the resulting value.

Thus:
x = 10
x = x + 1
leaves x equal to 11.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
4.3 Program state
The state of a program consists, roughly speaking, of the information that determines the program’s current condition.
For a simple program, this may include the values associated with its variables.
Consider:
x = 10
y = x
x = 20
After these statements:
x → 20
y → 10
The assignment to x changed the program state. It did not change what y refers to.
This is one reason it is useful to distinguish programming variables from mathematical variables.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
section: 5.1 Types are part of the computational model

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
7.2 Converting decimal to binary
To express a positive integer in binary, we can decompose it into powers of 2.
For example,
\[
42=32+8+2
\]
or
\[
42=2^5+2^3+2^1.
\]
Therefore:
\[
42=101010_2.
\]
The positions corresponding to \(2^5,2^3,2^1\) contain 1s; the others contain 0s.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
9.1 Unsigned integers
If all 256 patterns are used for nonnegative integers, the values are:
\[
0,1,\ldots,255.
\]
The largest value is therefore
\[
2^8-1=255.
\]
In general, an unsigned \(b\)-bit integer has range
\[
0,\ldots,2^b-1.
\]

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
9.2 What happens outside the range?
If a system uses an 8-bit unsigned integer, there is no representation for 256.
In some low-level programming environments, arithmetic can overflow and wrap around.
For example, an 8-bit unsigned representation may behave as though
\[
255+1=0
\]
because the result (256) corresponds to the bit pattern
00000000
after discarding the ninth bit.
Python’s ordinary int does not behave this way.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
section: 10.1 Arbitrary precision does not mean infinite precision
text:
10.1 Arbitrary precision does not mean infinite precision
Python’s integer type can grow as necessary, but there are still physical limits.
A sufficiently large integer requires:

more memory;
more computational time;
potentially more storage.

Thus:

The programming language can provide an abstraction that hides hardware-level limits without eliminating the underlying physical limits.

This distinction becomes particularly important when we study numerical computing.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
11.1 The largest and smallest values
The largest value is:
01111111
which is 127.
The smallest is:
10000000
which represents -128.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
11.2 Two’s complement and arithmetic
The two’s-complement representation is designed so that ordinary binary addition can be used for both positive and negative numbers, subject to the limits of the fixed-width representation.
For example:
  00000101   =  5
+ 11111110   = -2
-----------
  00000011   =  3
The representation makes arithmetic efficient in hardware.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
11.3 Integer overflow
With fixed-width signed integers, arithmetic can leave the representable range.
For an 8-bit signed integer:
01111111 = 127
Adding 1 produces:
10000000
which represents -128.
This is integer overflow.
Python’s int deliberately avoids this particular behavior by allowing the integer representation to grow.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
14.1 Normalized values
For a normalized binary floating-point value, the significand is conventionally represented with a leading 1.
Conceptually:
\[
1.f_2 \times 2^e.
\]
The leading 1 does not need to be stored explicitly, which provides an additional effective bit of precision.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
Precision
Precision concerns how finely numbers can be distinguished relative to their magnitude.
Binary64 has approximately 15–17 significant decimal digits of precision.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
Range
Range concerns how large or small a representable number can be.
For typical binary64:
\[
\text{maximum finite value}
\approx
1.8\times10^{308}.
\]
The smallest positive normal number is approximately:
\[
2.2\times10^{-308}.
\]
These are different concepts.
A system can have a large numerical range while still having limited precision.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
Conditioning
Conditioning concerns the sensitivity of the mathematical problem itself to perturbations in the input.
A problem is ill-conditioned if small changes in the input can produce large changes in the correct answer.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
Stability
Stability concerns the behavior of the algorithm used to solve the problem.
A stable algorithm tends not to introduce excessive additional error.
This distinction is important:

An ill-conditioned problem can be difficult even with a perfect algorithm.

and:

A well-conditioned problem can be ruined by an unstable algorithm.

We will return to these ideas later in the course.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
34.1 Testing known results
For example:
def sum_of_squares(n):
    total = 0

    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        total += i**2

    return total
We can test:
assert sum_of_squares(1) == 1
assert sum_of_squares(2) == 5
assert sum_of_squares(3) == 14

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
38.1 Mathematical objects versus representations
A mathematical integer is an abstract object.
A computer stores a finite representation of that integer.
A mathematical real number is an abstract object.
A computer generally stores an approximation to that real number.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
38.2 Programs versus mathematical expressions
A mathematical expression describes a relationship or value.
A program is a sequence of instructions that changes computational state.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
38.3 Exact versus approximate computation
Integer calculations can often be exact within the range of the representation.
Floating-point calculations are generally approximate.

title: Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
Lecture 1 — Foundations, Computation & Binary Representations
text:
38.5 Testing matters
A program producing output is not evidence that the output is correct.
Testing should be deliberate and systematic.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
In Lecture 1, we considered individual computational values: integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and Boolean values. We also introduced a central idea that will recur throughout the course:

A computer does not manipulate mathematical objects directly. It executes algorithms using finite representations of information.

Today we move from individual values to collections of information and to programs that can make decisions and repeat operations.
The central questions are:

How should a collection of information be represented?
How do we access individual elements?
How do we add, remove, or modify information?
How do we associate one piece of information with another?
How do we express repeated computation?
How do we make a program behave differently depending on its input?
How do we turn an informal problem into a precise algorithm?

A useful way to think about today’s material is:
Information
    ↓
Data structure
    ↓
Operations on the data
    ↓
Control flow
    ↓
Algorithm
    ↓
Implementation
    ↓
Testing / validation
The choice of data structure is not merely a programming-language detail. It is part of the solution to the problem.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
2.1 ASCII
The original ASCII standard assigns numeric codes to a relatively small set of characters.
For example:
ord("A")
returns:
65
and:
chr(65)
returns:
'A'
ASCII is useful but limited. It was designed around the needs of English-language text and contains only a small number of characters.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
2.2 Unicode
Unicode is a much larger standard intended to provide a consistent representation for characters used by languages around the world.
A Unicode code point is a number assigned to a character.
For example:
ord("A")
gives the Unicode code point for A, while:
ord("é")
gives the code point for é.
The important distinction is:

A Unicode code point identifies a character; it is not necessarily the same thing as the bytes used to store that character.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
2.3 UTF-8
UTF-8 is an encoding that maps Unicode characters to sequences of bytes.
For example:
"A".encode("utf-8")
produces a one-byte representation, while a character such as é requires more than one byte:
"é".encode("utf-8")
The resulting object is a sequence of bytes.
We can convert those bytes back into a string:
b = "é".encode("utf-8")
b.decode("utf-8")
The distinction among character, code point, and byte is important when working with files and data.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
3.1 Indexing
If:
s = "Python"
then:
index:    0   1   2   3   4   5
          P   y   t   h   o   n
Thus:
s[0]
is "P" and:
s[5]
is "n".
Negative indices count from the end:
s[-1]
is "n".

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
3.2 Slicing
A slice selects a portion of a sequence.
s[1:4]
returns:
'yth'
The general form is:
s[start:stop]
The starting index is included, but the stopping index is excluded.
This convention is extremely useful because the length of:
s[a:b]
is normally:
b - a
provided the indices are valid.
We will see the same convention with lists and other sequences.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
3.3 Strings are immutable
Python strings are immutable. Once a string object has been created, its characters cannot be changed in place.
For example, this is not allowed:
s = "Python"
s[0] = "J"
Instead, we create a new string:
s = "J" + s[1:]
Immutability is an important concept because different data structures have different rules about whether their contents can be changed.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
3.4 String methods
Strings have many useful methods:
text = "  Hello, World!  "

text.strip()
text.lower()
text.upper()
text.replace("World", "Python")
text.split(",")
These methods are particularly useful when processing real-world data, where text is often messy.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
5.1 Indexing and slicing
Lists use the same indexing and slicing conventions as strings:
temperatures[0]
temperatures[-1]
temperatures[1:4]
This is not accidental. Both strings and lists are examples of sequences.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
5.2 Lists are mutable
Unlike strings, lists can be modified.
temperatures[0] = 73
We can append an element:
temperatures.append(76)
or remove an element:
temperatures.pop()

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
5.3 Lists and mathematical vectors
It is tempting to think of a Python list as a mathematical vector:
\[
x =
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
x_2\\
\vdots\\
x_n
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This analogy is useful, but it has limits.
A Python list is a general-purpose container. It does not automatically perform vectorized mathematical operations.
For example:
x = [1, 2, 3]
does not behave like a NumPy vector. This distinction will become important when we study NumPy.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
7.1 Dictionaries as mappings
Mathematically, a dictionary is naturally related to the idea of a mapping or function.
For example:
\[
f(\text{student ID}) = \text{student name}.
\]
A dictionary can implement a finite version of this idea:
names = {
    101: "Ada",
    102: "Grace",
    103: "Alan"
}
Then:
names[102]
returns "Grace".

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
11.1 Boolean operators
Python provides:
and
or
not
For example:
x > 0 and x < 10
means that both conditions must be true.
We can also write:
0 < x < 10
which is Python’s chained-comparison syntax.
The mathematical connection is direct:
\[
0 < x < 10.
\]
But remember that a Boolean expression is evaluated by the program and produces a Boolean value.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
12.1 Mathematical logic and program logic
A conditional statement is closely related to mathematical reasoning.
For example:

If \(x > 0\), then \(x^2 > 0\).

A program can operationalize a similar logical condition:
if x > 0:
    ...
But a program must also specify what action to take when the condition is true or false.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
13.1 Accumulating a result
One common pattern is to maintain a running total.
numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8]

total = 0

for x in numbers:
    total = total + x

print(total)
This is a computational implementation of:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.
\]
The program state changes after every iteration.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Specification
State precisely what the program should accomplish.
For example:

Given a nonempty sequence of numbers, return its largest element.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
Algorithm
Describe how to accomplish the specification.
Set current maximum to first element.

For every remaining element:
    if the element exceeds current maximum:
        replace current maximum.

Return current maximum.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
23.1 Why complexity matters
We do not need advanced computer science to see the practical implication.
If an algorithm requires approximately:
\[
n
\]
operations and another requires approximately:
\[
n^2
\]
operations, then increasing the input size by a factor of 100 changes the work by approximately:

factor of 100 for the first algorithm;
factor of 10,000 for the second.

Thus algorithmic choices can become consequential very quickly.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
26.1 Off-by-one errors
Because Python uses zero-based indexing and excludes the stop value in slices and range(), it is easy to write:
range(1, 10)
when you intended to include 10.
Always check the first and last values explicitly.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
26.2 Mutability confusion
Lists can be changed; strings and tuples cannot.
Knowing whether a data structure is mutable helps explain unexpected behavior.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
26.3 Confusing position and identity
A list is naturally indexed by position:
values[3]
A dictionary is naturally indexed by a key:
prices["AAPL"]
Choosing the wrong structure can make a problem unnecessarily difficult.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
text:
26.4 Infinite loops
A while loop must eventually make its condition false if termination is expected.

title: Lecture 2 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Control Flow
section: 26.5 Assuming code that runs is correct
text:
26.5 Assuming code that runs is correct
As emphasized in Lecture 1:

The absence of an error message is not evidence that the result is correct.

A program can execute perfectly while implementing the wrong algorithm.

text:
Course Description
This course provides a fast-paced introduction to programming and computational methods for graduate study in mathematics and statistics. We will use Python and R to develop practical programming skills while also introducing fundamental ideas from computer science, numerical computing, data management, and reproducible research.
The course emphasizes problem solving and computational thinking rather than memorization of language syntax. Topics include programming fundamentals, data structures, algorithms, numerical representation and error, data manipulation and visualization, simulation, statistical computing, software organization, version control, testing and debugging, and reproducible computational workflows.
An important goal is to prepare students not only to write programs for this course, but also to approach computational problems effectively in subsequent coursework, research, and professional settings. We will therefore discuss practices used in real computational work, including organizing projects, managing dependencies and data, writing maintainable code, testing programs, documenting work, and using Git and GitHub.
The course uses Python and R throughout. Students will generally learn concepts first through Python and then see how similar computational ideas are expressed in R.

Students should be comfortable with algebra and basic mathematical notation and should be prepared to learn programming at a relatively rapid pace.

Course Organization
The course is organized around several broad themes:

Programming fundamentals: variables, types, expressions, control flow, functions, data structures, and program state.
Computational foundations: algorithms, binary and numerical representation, floating-point arithmetic, numerical error, and computational complexity.
Data and scientific computing: working with arrays and data frames, data cleaning and transformation, visualization, simulation, and numerical computation.
Statistical computing: applying computational methods to statistical problems and working with real datasets.
Software and data practices: testing, debugging, documentation, project organization, version control, dependency management, and reproducibility.
Python and R: learning the common computational ideas that underlie both languages while becoming comfortable using each language in practice.

The course will move quickly. Class meetings will combine short lectures with live coding, demonstrations, and exercises that students complete individually or collaboratively.

title: MATH 5200: Computing Using R & Python

Course Philosophy
The goal of this course is not to memorize Python or R syntax. The goal is to become someone who can solve problems computationally.
A typical computational workflow looks something like:

Problem → algorithm → implementation → testing → analysis → results

We will pay attention to every part of this process. In particular, students will learn to recognize that producing an answer is not necessarily the same thing as producing a correct, reliable, or reproducible computational result.
Students are encouraged to ask questions, experiment, make mistakes, and use computational tools to investigate ideas. At the same time, submitted work should demonstrate that students understand the code they write and the methods they use.
